title: Merit Restored or Rights Erased? Education Department Expands Medical School Probes
subtitle: The Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights has launched investigations into five medical schools for alleged racial discrimination in admissions, part of a broader campaign affecting more than 50 universities nationwide.

conservative.headline: Ed Department Cracks Down on Med Schools Still Picking Doctors by Race
conservative.byline: As seen on Washington Times, Breitbart, Washington Examiner
paragraphs: The Trump administration is finally doing what the Supreme Court ordered: ending racial discrimination in higher education. After years of medical schools flouting the law and selecting future doctors based on skin color rather than qualifications, the Department of Education and Justice Department have launched sweeping investigations into institutions that continue to prioritize racial quotas over merit.

Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey made the stakes crystal clear in announcing the investigations. As The Washington Times reported, she declared that "your race should not decide whether or not you can study medicine, yet many schools seem to be more focused on meeting racial quotas than selecting individuals who have earned entrance based on merit." This statement captures what conservatives have been saying for years: diversity, equity, and inclusion programs are just racial discrimination by another name.

The Department of Justice has been equally aggressive in pursuing these violations. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon didn't mince words when explaining why fifteen new investigations into medical school admissions were necessary, noting that "many of America's top medical schools appear more concerned about the demographics of their incoming classes than training students to succeed in the profession." When medical schools care more about checking racial boxes than ensuring competence, patient care suffers.

The evidence of ongoing discrimination is damning. In July 2024, the Department of Education announced that five medical schools were under investigation for racial discrimination: Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth, Brody School of Medicine at East Carolina University, Saint Louis University School of Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, and William Carey University College of Osteopathic Medicine. Each receives millions in federal taxpayer funding while potentially violating civil rights law.

Medical professionals are speaking out about the danger these policies pose. Rep. Greg Murphy, a North Carolina Republican who is also a practicing physician, testified before Congress that diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts represent the "most divisive, horrible cancer" in medical school. When a doctor says DEI is a cancer infecting medical education, Americans should pay attention.

The settlement with UC Davis Medical School demonstrates how brazen these institutions have become. In that case, Dhillon noted the school showed "unabashed contempt for the rule of law and plain disregard for the potential public health consequences of putting race over merit, skill, and competence." This isn't about diversity—it's about schools deliberately choosing less qualified applicants based solely on race.

Watchdog groups are ensuring these discriminatory practices can't continue in secret. Kurt Miceli, Medical Director at Do No Harm, emphasized that "schools and health systems cannot be allowed to fly under the radar and continue these obviously discriminatory practices, especially when they have the vital job of producing our future doctors." Transparency and accountability are exactly what's needed.

The Supreme Court ruled that race-based admissions are unconstitutional, yet medical schools across America have continued using racial preferences in defiance of the law. The Trump administration's investigations aren't a purge—they're enforcement of civil rights protections that apply to Americans of all races. When choosing the doctors who will save lives, merit must be the only standard that matters.

liberal.headline: Trump's Civil Rights Office Targets Medical Schools in Widening Anti-Diversity Purge
liberal.byline: As seen on CNN, Stanford Daily, Inside Higher Ed
paragraphs: The Trump administration has weaponized the federal civil rights apparatus to wage war on diversity in higher education, launching investigations into medical schools as part of a coordinated campaign to dismantle programs that address centuries of racial inequity. What the administration calls "enforcing civil rights" is actually an authoritarian assault on academic freedom and an attempt to preserve white privilege in the medical profession.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta exposed the true nature of these investigations in his response to the federal probe of Stanford Medical School. As The Stanford Daily reported, Bonta condemned the Trump administration's "fishing expedition — demanding unprecedented amounts of data from our colleges and universities under the guise of enforcing civil rights law." This isn't about protecting students from discrimination; it's about intimidating institutions that dare to acknowledge America's racist history.

The investigations are transparently political. During a House hearing on the issue, Democrats called out the Republican charade for what it is. House Democrats noted that "now, instead of helping Americans, Republicans are sitting here targeting medical schools." While working families struggle with healthcare costs and medical debt, Republicans are obsessed with punishing universities for trying to train a diverse physician workforce.

Civil rights organizations see through the administration's rhetoric. Thomas A. Saenz, president of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, delivered a scathing assessment of the federal government's settlement with UC Davis. Saenz stated that the agreement "represents a federal government that seeks to preserve white privilege rather than to secure equal opportunity," noting that the administration coerced an agreement that "goes beyond applicable constitutional restrictions."

The scope of this campaign is staggering. In June 2024, the Department of Justice announced fifteen new investigations into medical school admissions, and by July, the Education Department had added five more schools to the list. More than 50 universities are now under investigation in what amounts to a coordinated federal harassment campaign against institutions committed to educational equity.

The real-world consequences of this purge will be devastating. Medical schools have worked for decades to address the stark reality that physicians of color are dramatically underrepresented in medicine, contributing to health disparities that literally cost lives in minority communities. Studies consistently show that patients have better health outcomes when they can see doctors who understand their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences. By dismantling diversity initiatives, the Trump administration is effectively ensuring that medicine remains a predominantly white profession serving an increasingly diverse nation.

The administration's claims about "merit" are particularly insidious because they ignore how systemic racism has created unequal access to educational opportunities from birth. Wealthy white students have access to test prep, legacy admissions, and well-funded schools that poor students and students of color don't enjoy. When Republicans talk about "merit," they're really talking about preserving a system rigged in favor of privilege.

This isn't about civil rights enforcement—it's about civil rights destruction. The Trump administration is using the threat of federal investigations to terrorize any institution that tries to address America's legacy of racism and inequality. Medical schools that sought to train doctors capable of serving all Americans are now being punished for that commitment. The message is clear: in Trump's America, diversity is a crime and equality is the enemy.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin
paragraphs: Both sides are presenting selective versions of events. Conservatives portray all diversity programs as illegal racial quotas, while liberals characterize legitimate civil rights enforcement as pure political persecution. Here is what we actually know.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ The investigations are real and expanding: In June 2024, the Department of Justice announced 15 new investigations into potential race discrimination in medical school admissions. In July 2024, the Department of Education launched investigations into five additional schools: Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth, Brody School of Medicine at East Carolina University, Saint Louis University School of Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, and William Carey University College of Osteopathic Medicine.

✓ The Supreme Court ruling matters: In June 2023, the Supreme Court ruled in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard that race-conscious admissions violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Universities can no longer use race as a factor in admissions decisions. This ruling is binding law, regardless of one's opinion about its wisdom or fairness.

✓ Medical schools did use race in admissions: Prior to the Supreme Court ruling, many medical schools explicitly considered race as one factor among many in holistic admissions processes. The question is whether schools have fully abandoned these practices post-ruling, or whether they've found workarounds.

✓ Both political parties have used civil rights enforcement selectively: Every administration prioritizes certain civil rights issues over others based on its political philosophy. Democratic administrations have historically focused on discrimination against minorities, while Republican administrations often emphasize claims of reverse discrimination. This pattern predates Trump.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: All diversity programs are illegal racial quotas. Reality: The Supreme Court ruling prohibits using race as a factor in individual admissions decisions, but it doesn't ban all diversity initiatives. Schools can still conduct outreach to underrepresented communities, provide socioeconomic-based assistance, and consider applicants' individual experiences with discrimination in essays. The line between legal and illegal practices is complex and fact-specific.

⚠️ Implication: Merit-based admissions previously didn't exist. Reality: Medical school admissions have always been holistic, considering grades, test scores, research experience, clinical exposure, personal statements, letters of recommendation, and interviews. Race was one factor among dozens. Even now, applicants aren't admitted purely on MCAT scores and GPAs—medical schools still use subjective judgments about character, resilience, and potential.

✓ Fair Point: Some medical schools did appear to use explicit racial targets or preferences that likely violated equal protection principles even before the Supreme Court ruling. If investigations reveal evidence of actual quotas or mechanical racial preferences, those practices were indeed unlawful.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: These investigations are purely political persecution with no legitimate basis. Reality: While the Trump administration is clearly prioritizing this issue for ideological reasons, the legal authority for these investigations exists. If medical schools are continuing to use race-conscious admissions in defiance of the Supreme Court ruling, that would constitute actual civil rights violations. The legitimacy depends on whether the investigations uncover genuine evidence of prohibited practices.

⚠️ Implication: Diversity programs don't raise any constitutional concerns. Reality: The Supreme Court's ruling represents settled constitutional law, at least for now. Six justices concluded that race-based admissions violate equal protection. One can disagree with this interpretation, but it's currently binding precedent. Schools must operate within these constitutional constraints.

✓ Fair Point: The administration's rhetoric and the scope of investigations do suggest an agenda beyond simple law enforcement. Demanding "unprecedented amounts of data" from dozens of schools simultaneously, as California AG Rob Bonta described, could constitute regulatory harassment even if each individual investigation has some legal justification.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

What neither side adequately addresses is the underlying tension: medical schools face a genuine dilemma. Research shows that physician diversity improves health outcomes for underserved populations, yet the legal tools previously used to increase diversity are now prohibited. Schools must find new approaches that serve public health goals while complying with constitutional requirements.

The investigations will ultimately turn on specific evidence: Are schools using prohibited racial preferences, or are they using permissible diversity strategies? Have they genuinely changed their practices post-ruling, or are they using pretextual workarounds? These are factual questions that political rhetoric from neither side can answer.

The Bottom Line: The Trump administration has legal authority to investigate potential civil rights violations in medical school admissions, and some schools may indeed be violating the Supreme Court's ruling. However, the simultaneous investigation of dozens of institutions, the inflammatory rhetoric from officials, and the timing suggest this is also a political campaign against diversity initiatives more broadly. Both the legal violations and the political motivations can be true at the same time.
